doc.title: Jerry Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe and Christian Goodwillie, via Zoom, June 30, 2021

title: Danny Ray Thompson, Pharaoh's Den and negotiating prices
summary: He explains Thompson's name, the Pharaoh's Den store, and Thompson's price negotiations when delivering records.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: That’s four dollars and forty-nine cents, not four hundred and forty-nine.
Now they go for four hundred and forty-nine dollars. You’re right, Monk. No they went for a regular price.
Wow. Did Danny Ray Thompson, he also ran that Pharaoh’s Den store, right?
Yeah. In Germantown. It was like a grocery store. I don’t even know.
Okay. You never went in there?
No I never went in there.
Okay. So you started re-issuing these Sun Ra records while Sun Ra was still alive. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

Of course. By the way as far as Danny Thompson goes I’d like to tell one more anecdote. When he would bring records into the store, sometimes, you know, Sun Ra would come along with him you know, in the Cadillac. And that’s why Sun Ra, you know, came into the store, and let’s go down to Third Street, and Sun Ra would look around and then Danny would have a private session with me. There was no standard price. Every load of records was his own negotiation. I had to do it over and over again every time I saw them. It was exhausting sometimes. Danny would say, “Jerry we’ve got something special here, I’m going to have to charge you more.” “What? What do you mean you’re going to have to charge me more?” He says, “Yeah, this is special. You should only sell these to certain customers. Not everybody can handle it and we’ve got to charge more.” This is the — every time he brought in records we went through this kind of stuff. But it was fun, it was endearing, it was absolutely endearing and people negotiating with me generally has never been endearing, okay, but in this case it was.
